text: Considering the two main components of a QSAR model, the molecular representation and the model architecture, we sought to understand how each contributes to both predictive performance and noise robustness.
ANOVA decomposition divides the variance between model family, model architecture within its family, molecular representation, the pairing of the two, the replicate, and a residual.

We ran this decomposition for Gaussian noise, the standard model, as well as methods whose injected noise is related to the feature space, grouped-wider and grouped-shifted (Figure [REF], Table [REF]).
For predictive performance measured in R^2 at a noise level of 1.0, model family and molecular representation account for comparable shares of the variance, 26.6\% and 29.0\% under Gaussian noise.

However, for noise robustness, quantified by the normalized area under the R^2 retention curve (; higher values indicate greater robustness), model family accounts for 47.2\% of the variance while molecular representation for 8.1\%.
This pattern is observed across noise conditions and makes sense, as label noise does not impact the features.

The interaction between model and molecular representation explains 19.9\% of the variance in , more than twice the 8.1\% explained by representation alone, meaning representation acts on noise robustness mainly through the model it is paired with.
As such, we primarily compare representations within each model.
We compare the variance decomposition on both clean and noisy labels (Figure [REF]a).
For predictive performance, the artificial label noise lowers the impact of the choice of model family, while the replicate and residual take more.
This means that the variance is left more up to chance and to the underlying variation within the data itself with label noise, which is the expected behavior.
Robustness divides the variance a bit differently.
Representation explains 8.1\% of the variance in , against 31.1\% of clean R^2, while model family rises to 47.2\%.
The replicate nearly disappears from , likely because each replicate's curve is divided by that replicate's own clean R^2, so a difficult split lowers both and cancels out.
We include two terms which stem from the data rather than the model, the residual and replicate terms.
The replicate measures how much of the variance can be attributed to the train and test split, which in this case is a scaffold split.
On QM9 we replicated each experiment 10 times with different random draws of N=10,000, each time giving a new scaffold split.
On the assay datasets, a replicate refers to one of the five scaffold CV folds.
A large replicate term in ANOVA indicates that the folds differ from one another.
The residual is variance that no other term accounts for.

While we observe similar patterns between noise conditions, the predictive performance of grouped-shifted noise in particular varies significantly between replicates, resulting in a larger share for the replicate.
We find that 28.4\% of the variance in and 51.0\% of the variance in R^2 are due to the replicate, with model family falling to 32.7\% and 8.4\%.
This indicates that the offset applied to each scaffold may account for more of the variance in both R^2 and .
The variance decomposition tells us what aspect of QSAR modeling affects predictive performance and robustness, however it does not tell us about the characteristics of individual models.
All models' performance degrades as the labels get increasingly corrupted with noise (Figure [REF]).
The loss remains small until the artificial noise reaches about half the spread of the clean training labels, and then it begins to drop.
The rate it drops and the quantity of noise retained is not necessarily correlated to the model's predictive performance on clean labels.
Across the 13 base models under Gaussian noise at ECFP4, clean R^2 and rank in opposite directions at a Spearman correlation of -0.10 (p = 0.73) (Figure [REF]).
If anything, the lower a model's predictive performance on clean labels, the less it has to lose as the labels get noisier.
The link between predictive performance and noise robustness can be examined by model family (Figure [REF]).
The forests, boosted trees, SVM, and GP all retain relatively high predictive performance on clean labels while maintaining relatively strong robustness to noise.
The plain NNs and BNNs are among the highest in predictive performance on clean labels, and are the four least robust.
The two variational networks sit between these groups, with lower predictive performance on clean labels and middling noise robustness.
Standard feed-forward networks can make strong predictions under clean labels, however they are not a safe bet under noisy ones.
NGBoost is a standout case in the sense it is highly dependent on its paired molecular representation.
Under Gaussian noise it has the highest on every one of the six representations, yet also the lowest in predictive performance on four of the six representations.
It is one of the worst performing models with respect to R^2 on clean data.
Its high robustness is partially due to the fact that when you start with a low predictive performance, you don't have as much to lose.
However, it maintains shallow robustness curves across representations.
On ECFP4 NGBoost's predictive performance ranks lowest up to a noise level of 0.75 and stays in the lower half at every noise level.
However, on PDV it starts second lowest and ends highest, surpassing the other models between noise levels 1.0 and 1.5.
So when paired with the right features, NGBoost has the potential to make better predictions under higher quantities of label noise.
On grouped-shifted noise, RF has higher values than NGBoost on ECFP4, Avalon and ChemBERTa.
Even then, NGBoost reports the highest noise robustness for PDV, MHG-GNN and Sort \& Slice.
While NGBoost performs well under higher label noise, LightGBM performs well under smaller quantities of noise.
Its performance drops sharply after noise level 1.0.

As we've seen, the choice of representation can have an impact on noise robustness, but that impact is determined by model family, represented by the interaction term between model and representation in Figure [REF].
Some models are more impacted by representation than others, though.
In general, networks span a wider range of across the six representations than any of the other models.
Between ECFP4 and PDV under Gaussian noise, the four plain and Bayesian networks differ by between 0.037 and 0.065 of , while no tree or kernel model shifts by more than 0.011.
VBLLs are an exception, as no two variational networks differ by more than 0.019.

To further explore the impact of model architecture on noise robustness, we examined deterministic and probabilistic variants of the same core model architecture.
The hypothesis was that a model that reports a distribution rather than a point value may be more robust to small amounts of injected label noise.
We compared variants across three sets of base models: two NNs labeled NN- and NN- and RF (Figure [REF]).
For each NN, we transform a standard deterministic network into a BNN.
The BNNs with a variance head run at different settings from their Bayesian bases, so they are compared only for uncertainty.
We compared RF to its probabilistic counterpart, QRF, with the same baseline architecture and hyperparameters.
Comparisons of this nature are only possible when the variants carry the same underlying settings (Additional files [REF] and [REF]).
NN- and BNN- therefore share one setting, as do NN- and BNN-, and QRF is compared with a random forest of the same 300 trees (Additional file [REF]).
We compare RF and QRF directly with the same underlying architecture.
QRF had lower on QM9 under Gaussian and grouped-shifted noise on every representation, and changed it little under grouped-wider noise, with almost no change in clean R^2 (Figure [REF]).
On the assay datasets QRF was less robust than RF under grouped-shifted noise on every dataset and representation, and under Gaussian noise on LogD and hERG K_i (Additional file [REF]).
Under grouped-wider noise it was more robust on Caco-2 and mixed elsewhere.

The Bayesian transformations that we used to transform feed-forward deterministic NNs into probabilistic ones produced a slightly larger , but only because they lowered predictive performance on clean labels.
BNN- kept more than NN- in most combinations on every assay dataset, and BNN- on all assay datasets.
On QM9 the Bayesian transformations made no significant change on either predictive performance or for either network.
Until now we've discussed how much predictive capabilities a model is able to retain while its training labels are corrupted with noise.
Now, we consider how confident the model reports its own predictions are in the presence of noise, and whether or not those estimates match the increased label noise.
[CIT] found that the mean predicted uncertainty derived from the GPs increases with the amount of label noise in the training data.
We go beyond the population level and instead ask if a model's per-sample uncertainty tracks label noise.
One key sign that a model is able to handle noise is its ability to track it, represented by the per-sample Spearman correlation between predicted uncertainty and noise magnitude.
As expected, mean predicted uncertainty is positively correlated with Gaussian label noise for most models and representations (Table [REF]).
There are a few exceptions, namely BNN- on PDV and VBLL- (het.) on Avalon for QM9.

BNN- fails to rise in at least one fold on every assay dataset, and both full-BNNs with a variance head fail on MHG-GNN for hERG K_i, and BNN- with a variance head also fails on ChemBERTa and on Caco-2.
[CIT]'s finding therefore holds for almost every probabilistic model on the computed property, and for most of them on measured labels.
While this tells us that the models are reportedly less certain under noisy data, we don't know what the model is attributing this uncertainty to.
To answer this question, we decompose uncertainty estimates into their aleatoric and epistemic components wherever possible.

We expect to see aleatoric uncertainty rise with injected label noise, while the epistemic component should remain relatively constant, as it is the aleatoric component that describes uncertainty in the underlying data.
The models whose frameworks allowed for this decomposition include full-BNNs with a variance head, the heteroscedastic GP, and QRF (Table [REF]).
The two heteroscedastic VBLL networks also report both components, and they separate them more often than any other model, though not on every dataset and representation.
They are not drawn in the figures, as they were not scored out of fold.
The full-BNNs with a variance head behave as expected (Figure [REF]), the epistemic component grows by at most 0.43 of the aleatoric growth in every configuration where the ratio can be computed.

Despite QRF's strong predictive performance and noise robustness, both of its aleatoric and epistemic components rise with noise and on some representations, the epistemic component actually rises at a faster rate.
Unlike the predictive performance and robustness, the representation actually dictates whether decomposition works.
For QRF, the epistemic growth is 0.61 to 1.14 times the aleatoric growth on the three fingerprints, 1.02 to 1.44 times on PDV, and 1.29 to 2.04 times on ChemBERTa and MHG-GNN.

Under Gaussian noise the heteroscedastic GP keeps its epistemic growth below a quarter of its aleatoric growth on PDV, ChemBERTa and MHG-GNN except MHG-GNN on QM9, but not on ECFP4 under grouped-shifted noise, where the two grow by similar amounts.

The noise conditions follow the pattern found in robustness, the three conditions which alternate the noise distribution show similar decompositions to those under Gaussian noise, while grouped-shifted raises the epistemic share of the heteroscedastic GP and of QRF in every pairing of dataset and representation.
This scaffold family-based offset may be appearing as structure in the data rather than label noise to the models.
The aleatoric component indicates that label noise increased, but it doesn't tell us by how much (Figure [REF]).
For each unit of added noise it rises by roughly 0.4 to 1 unit, depending on model, dataset and representation.
The aleatoric component can therefore compare noise between datasets or noise levels, but it does not estimate a dataset's internal error.
Uncertainty estimation breaks under censoring as the process of clipping the labels narrows their spread, which in turn shrinks the total uncertainty.
None of the models tested treat a clipped label as a noisy one, so they actually grow more confident while losing information.
Finally, we ask whether a model's uncertainty on one molecule tracks the noise on that molecule's label.
We assess this using the Spearman correlation between predicted uncertainty and the size of the injected noise over out-of-fold training molecules.
Since Gaussian, Laplace, Student-t and grouped-shifted conditions add noise from the same scale to every label, there is not much for uncertainty to find.

It's the same situation with outlier noise, under which a tenth of the data is chosen at random for extra noise, and with grouped-wider in which each scaffold family falls in a single fold, so a model makes predictions based on unseen scaffolds and has no basis for estimating uncertainty.
The only case where per-sample uncertainty tracking is possible is censoring, as the noise is dependent on the value of the label itself.
The correlations are then large and mostly negative, meaning the model is least uncertain on the labels that were clipped most.

On QM9 with half the labels clipped, on PDV, they run from -0.84 to -0.80 across folds for NGBoost and from -0.47 to -0.41 for the GP, and on LogD with half the labels clipped every fold of every model except the two GPs is at -0.29 or lower.
We divided each molecule's error by its uncertainty and found that the division ranked the clipped labels better than the error alone on QM9 and on most of LogD.
Models are most confident on the clipped labels, probably because the clipping piles many labels into one value, which the model learns to tightly predict.

Ironically, per-molecule uncertainty can be used in reverse to identify clipped labels, as the labels a model is more certain about, especially when they fall in a certain range, are most likely to have been clipped.
We investigated how a variety of molecular representations and models perform under increasing label noise.

We used ANOVA variance decomposition across three noise conditions on four datasets to show that molecular representation accounts for a larger share of the variance in predictive performance than in robustness.
Robustness to label noise, as measured by , the normalized area under the R^2 retention curve, is more impacted by the choice of model.
The representation each model is paired with explains more variance than the representation alone.

As such, a representation should not be chosen independently of the model it will be used with, and some models benefit from alternative molecular representations across both predictive performance and noise robustness.
Model family was the primary factor in every decomposition except one, Caco-2 under grouped-shifted noise, where the scaffold fold took the larger share.
Grouped-shifted and censored noise, the two conditions in which the error is systematic, corrupt QSAR model predictions the most.
Changing the shape of the distribution from which noise is drawn barely has an impact on model performance, a conclusion which is in agreement with [CIT].

Low quantities of noise do not make much of an impact, on the HOMO--LUMO gap every base model keeps at least 93\% of its clean R^2 up to a noise level of 0.3, and grouped-shifted noise separates from the other conditions only from a level of 0.75 (Figure [REF]).
Models' performance begins to degrade more rapidly on the assay datasets than on the HOMO--LUMO gap, which makes sense as assay data contain inherent experimental noise.
Tree and kernel models maintained consistent across all representations, while the plain NNs and BNNs depended on the representation they were given, as did the predictive performance of NGBoost.
Across datasets and noise conditions, RF and QRF were reliably robust, although their predictive performance on clean labels was middling and on Caco-2 they struggled under Gaussian noise.
QRF was the slightly less robust of the two, falling below RF under Gaussian and grouped-shifted noise.
Other models performed well only under some conditions.

The GP had the highest predictive performance on clean labels and under independent noise but fell behind when the noise was shared within a scaffold family, NGBoost predicted well only with the right representation, and SVM led in predictive performance under scaffold-shared noise on some datasets.

Transforming a feed-forward network into a Bayesian one increased , but the Bayesian variants never predicted better at any noise level, so switching to a tree-based model is the stronger move under label noise.
With regard to uncertainty estimation, mean predicted uncertainty rose with label noise for almost every probabilistic model on QM9 and for the majority of models on the assay datasets.

Of the models whose aleatoric and epistemic components can be split per molecule, the BNNs with a variance head, the heteroscedastic GP and the heteroscedastic VBLL networks correctly attributed error from the injected noise as aleatoric, while QRF read that error as epistemic.
The success of a split is also dependent on the representation, which is not necessarily the case for predictive performance or noise robustness.

The aleatoric component rises by roughly 0.4 to 1 unit for each unit of noise added, so it can compare noise between datasets or between noise levels, but it does not measure a dataset's internal error.
Outside censoring, no model's per-sample uncertainty identified which labels had been corrupted.
Under censoring the models' most confident predictions are the clipped labels themselves, and dividing a molecule's error by its uncertainty picked out the clipped labels better than the error alone.
QM9 served as a relatively clean baseline as its properties are computed.
The assay datasets containing experimental measurements on the endpoints LogD, Caco-2 [CIT], and hERG K_i [CIT] are smaller and cover a more narrow range of the chemical space.
As the labels in these data are experimentally-derived and pooled from different laboratories, they contain some unknown amount of noise.
We are then adding artificial noise on top of the existing experimental noise.
These validation datasets supported the QM9 findings for the forests, with the boosted trees XGBoost and LightGBM the notable exceptions, degrading on the external datasets.
Future work should extend this type of noise robustness benchmarking to classification tasks and larger experimental datasets with better-known uncertainty estimates.

When training on noisy experimental data in the context of QSAR, it is important to keep in mind that a model's robustness to noise is primarily driven by its own mechanism of training, and to an extent the molecular representation the input data comes in, oftentimes with respect to the model.
Of the models tested, RF was the most consistent choice across the four datasets, ranking between first and eighth for on every dataset, representation and noise condition.
Where a predictive distribution is wanted, its probabilistic counterpart QRF maintains RF's predictive performance and nearly all of its noise robustness.
What QRF cannot do is say where that uncertainty came from.
Beyond the forests, the better choice depends on how much noise there is.
LightGBM and XGBoost predict well on clean labels and lose the most as noise rises, so they suit data you trust, while NGBoost and the VBLL networks start lower and hold what they have.
In this research, we define a noise level as a fraction of the spread of the clean training labels.
It is therefore relative to the dataset rather than an absolute measurement error, and cannot be mapped onto a given dataset exactly.
There are other mechanisms used to estimate the noise in a dataset directly.
When an assay's controls are available, the Z'-factor can be used to estimate noise [CIT].
You can also use screening data to test for row, column and plate effects, which produce systematic rather than independent error [CIT].
When you lack controls, replicates, and metadata, a label can be checked against the data itself.
Confident learning flags labels by comparing each label to what a model predicts for that molecule when it was left out of training [CIT].
You can use the point at which the model error matches the data's error to generate a predictive limit [CIT].
Beyond formal methods, you should consider how a dataset was assembled.
How many independent replicates were done, how many laboratories contributed, whether assay protocols were consistently applied, and how varied are the compounds in chemical space?
The first limitation of this study is data availability.
While HOMO--LUMO gap from QM9 is a good baseline as its computed labels carry no measurement error, it is only a single task.
As the noise is meant to replicate experimental data, this analysis would be improved by more quality-controlled, relatively clean and well-replicated experimental data across different targets.
However, data of that nature are hard to find publicly.
Second, is a ratio to clean R^2, so a model that starts from a low clean baseline has less to lose, and a few replicates scored above 1.05.
We tried other measures of noise robustness, but they were either too strongly correlated with clean R^2 or did not capture the right quantity.

The change in R^2 at a single noise level, for example, misses the shape of the curve. is not a perfect metric, but it describes the whole curve, and across the 13 base models it is unrelated to clean R^2.
Third, it is hard to draw conclusions that hold across so many conditions.
No model or representation wins everywhere, although RF comes closest.
When working with cheminformatics data, you don't know in advance how a model and representation will perform on the given prediction task.
The underlying data is probably noisy, but you don't know how noisy it is or what shape that noise takes.

Given that, our recommendation is to test a handful of models against a handful of representations rather than tuning a single pairing, since on every dataset the pairing explains more of the variance in robustness than the representation does alone.
The pattern of the noise should also guide that choice (Table [REF]).
The same preferences held on all four datasets.
Under Laplace, Student-t and outlier noise, RF was the most robust model and SVM was the second.
NGBoost lost under all three.
Under grouped-wider noise, QRF was the most robust model and SVM was close behind.
Of the boosted trees, XGBoost lost the most.
Grouped-shifted noise was the hardest condition.
Every model lost on every dataset and representation.
RF lost the least of the models that also predicted well, and the GP lost the most.
Gaussian noise was the only condition with a clear specialist.
NGBoost was the most robust model on the HOMO--LUMO gap under Gaussian noise with every representation, but not on Caco-2 or hERG K_i.
These results follow from the loss function each model fits.
NGBoost fits a per-molecule scale under a Gaussian likelihood, so it loses ground when the noise is not Gaussian.
SVM ignores residuals that fall inside its margin, so it gains under the same conditions.
QRF fits conditional quantiles, so a noisy scaffold family widens that family's interval without shifting the fit.
Each boosting stage fits the residuals of the stage before it, and those residuals are largest in the noisy families.
The GP is the most affected by error that is correlated with structure, because its kernel measures structure.
None of this matters if the data are clean, as little separated the models below a noise level of 0.3.
In this chapter each model was given a standard molecular representation, and the choice of representation explained relatively little of the variance in noise robustness.
We observe that this choice does impact the performance of different models to varying degrees, and the representations seem to capture different signals on each dataset that we tested.
Chapter [REF] asks how well these representations compare molecules on a single dataset.
General-purpose representations are built to span a broad range of chemical domains.

When your dataset covers only a small region of the chemical space, a lot of the features within these generalized representations become irrelevant, describing chemistry which is absent from the data at hand.
Pairwise comparisons of these representations rely on these irrelevant features.
To investigate similarity estimation, we first look at a simple measure: how many features vary within a dataset.
A single dataset often contains a set of relatively similar molecules.
Many features within a generalized representation contain information that describes all, or almost all, of the molecules in the set, failing to capture the variation between them.
We define a constant feature to be one that takes a single value in every molecule of a dataset and a near-constant feature to be one that carries the same value in at least 95\% of the molecules.

We counted constant and near-constant features from a set of representations (described in Table [REF]) across hERG K_i, Caco-2, LogD, QM9, MDR1--MDCK efflux, human liver microsome (HLM) clearance, rat liver microsome (RLM) clearance and the Lhasa hERG blocker training set.
MDR1--MDCK efflux and the two clearance datasets come from Biogen [CIT].
HLM clearance and the Lhasa hERG set are not in Table [REF]; their base representations are those with counts in Table [REF].
The substructure-based fingerprints have the most near-constant features.
The learned embeddings, which are taken from the last layers of a NN, have none except MHG-GNN (Tables [REF] and [REF], Figure [REF]).
ECFP4 is the worst offender.
On hERG K_i (1,412 molecules) 1,815 of the 2,048 features are near-constant.
That jumps to 1,997 out of 2,048 near-constant features for the HOMO--LUMO gap on QM9.
292 of MHG-GNN's 1,024 features are zero in every molecule across all seven datasets that used it.
They come directly from the saved encoder output rather than the data, and we have not looked into why.
These constant counts are sometimes filtered out by the distance.
Tanimoto similarity (Equation [REF]; the distance is 1-T) ignores bits off in both molecules, but a bit on in every molecule raises every molecule's measured similarity.
It does not use the 105 constant ECFP4 bits on hERG K_i.
Constant features add zero to a Euclidean or Manhattan distance; however, near-constant features are amplified.
That's great behavior if those features define an AC.
If not, they are contributing disproportionately to the measure of similarity.
A standard fingerprint- or descriptor-based representation can produce the same feature vector for two separate molecules.
In turn, models using this representation will produce a single prediction for the molecules with identical features.
Identical feature vectors do not always mean that the representation has merged two different molecules, since a dataset pooled from several sources can hold two measurements of the same molecule.
Many fingerprints are computed without stereochemistry [CIT].

In this research, ECFP4 is built with stereochemistry off, and the 2D descriptor sets (PDV, Mordred) also ignore it, so almost every molecule they produce identical representations for is a stereoisomer of another (Table [REF]).
Any representation that reads from these subsequently merges stereoisomers.
Additionally, methods using the Weisfeiler--Lehman relabeling scheme are bounded by the 1-Weisfeiler--Lehman test (Chapter [REF]), so some non-isomorphic graphs also receive the same vector.
This is seen in the graph-kernel features which tie 105 of 1,412 hERG K_i molecules, 56 of which differ only in stereochemistry and 49 in more than that.
Whether or not a learned embedding is able to differentiate stereoisomers is dependent on its input as well as its individual implementation.
SMI-TED, a pretrained SMILES encoder, ties 56 hERG K_i, 633 LogD and 177 Caco-2 molecules, all stereoisomers.
A tokenizer can drop stereochemistry prior to training.

The tokenizer of the ChemBERTa-77M-MTR checkpoint (ChemBERTa-2 in Table [REF], called ChemBERTa in Chapter [REF]) gives 72 of the 1,415 hERG K_i molecules of Chapter [REF] the same token sequence as another molecule.
Since stereoisomers can differ in measured activity [CIT], these representations lack potentially useful chemical information.
Two molecules are tied when a representation gives them exactly the same feature vector.
We counted ties on hERG K_i, LogD and Caco-2, for each dataset's base representations and augmentation features, the small feature sets added to the hybrid after it is built (Section [REF]).
No tie came from one compound listed twice (checked by InChIKey, which differs between stereoisomers) or from a row of zeros (Table [REF]).
Apart from the MACCS keys, most tied molecules are stereoisomers.
Atom pairs, PDV, Mordred and SMI-TED tie only stereoisomers, and ECFP4, Avalon and topological torsions add a few molecules that differ in more than their stereochemistry.
On hERG K_i, ECFP4, atom pairs, PDV, Mordred and SMI-TED tie the same 56 molecules, so joining any of these five representations leaves all 56 tied.
The WL graph kernel also ties 49 hERG K_i and 26 Caco-2 molecules that are not stereoisomers, and the MACCS keys tie the most molecules on every dataset, mostly not stereoisomers.
The 3D augmentation features and the learned embeddings ChemBERT, GROVER, MHG-GNN, MoLFormer and GraphMVP tie none, and joining all of a dataset's representations leaves no molecule tied.
A model has to give every molecule in a tied group the same prediction.
The best single prediction for a group is its mean label, so ties set an error that no model can go below,
where n is the number of molecules, G runs over the tied groups and y_G is the mean label of group G.

On hERG K_i this lowest error is at most 0.134 pK_i (MACCS keys), small next to the label standard deviation of 0.915 pK_i.
Single groups can still disagree by a lot.

Independent pK_i measurements of the same compound against the same target differ by 0.44 log units on average, with a standard deviation of 0.54 [CIT], so a gap larger than 0.54 inside a tied group is larger than typical measurement noise.
On hERG K_i, 6 of the 26 ECFP4 groups and 38 of the 153 MACCS groups differ by more than 0.54.
The widest ECFP4 group is a pair of stereoisomers 1.14 pK_i apart (Figure [REF]).
An ECFP4 model can at best predict their mean, 5.59 pK_i, which leaves each molecule 0.57 pK_i from its measured value.

Chapter [REF] gives the MoleculeACE definition of an activity cliff, which combines three similarity measures.
Here we use one.
Two molecules are similar if their ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity is at least 0.55 [CIT], and a molecule is a cliff if a similar molecule has a label that differs from its own by more than a set gap.
We chose the gap on each dataset so that 15\% of the molecules are cliffs, so the gap follows the spread of the labels (Table [REF]).
On hERG K_i the gap is 1.76 pK_i, and 211 of the 1,412 molecules are cliffs.
On QM9 only 1,093 pairs of the 9,978 molecules are similar, and the gap is 0.05 eV, 0.06 times the median absolute deviation of the labels.
On the three Biogen datasets (RLM clearance, MDR1--MDCK efflux and HLM clearance) it is 0.20 to 0.34 log units, 0.50 to 0.60 times the median absolute deviation.
The count of cliffs depends on the representation.
We kept each dataset's gap and replaced ECFP4 with each other base representation, calling similar the same number of closest pairs as ECFP4 does.
On hERG K_i the number of cliff molecules then ranges from 138 (atom pairs) to 267 (WL graph kernel).
Of the pairs that ECFP4 calls similar, only 57\% to 74\% are also among another representation's closest pairs, and on QM9 only 1\% to 24\% (Additional file [REF]).
We asked whether distance tracks label difference in two ways.

Over all pairs of molecules, we took the Spearman correlation between the distance of a pair and the absolute difference of its labels, a one-number summary of the neighborhood-behavior plot of [CIT]; datasets above 2,000 molecules were sampled down to 2,000.

Over each molecule's closest pairs only, we predicted each label as the mean label of the molecule's five nearest neighbors, taken from other scaffold groups, and took the Spearman correlation between predicted and measured labels.
Across the 70 combinations of dataset and representation, the all-pairs correlation ranged from -0.04 to 0.23 and was below 0.10 in 44 of them.
The five-neighbor prediction reached 0.29 to 0.89, higher than the all-pairs correlation in all 70 (Table [REF]; every representation is in Additional file [REF]).
On hERG K_i with ECFP4, the all-pairs correlation is 0.06, while the five-neighbor prediction reaches 0.72, with an RMSE of 0.63 pK_i against a label standard deviation of 0.92 pK_i.
Figure [REF] shows why the two differ.
Of the 996,166 hERG K_i pairs, 93\% have an ECFP4 Tanimoto similarity below 0.20, and only 1.1\% reach 0.55.
Over all pairs the median label difference is 0.81 pK_i, but above a similarity of about 0.4 it is 0.20 to 0.30 pK_i, although 8.3\% of the 774 pairs at 0.8 or above still differ by more than 1 pK_i.
Mordred shows the same pattern: the closest 5\% of pairs have a median difference of 0.44 pK_i, and every other 5\% has 0.78 to 1.11 pK_i.
The useful information sits in the few closest pairs.
The all-pairs correlation is set by the other 95\%, whereas the five-neighbor prediction uses only the closest pairs.

We compared the five nearest neighbors of each molecule, from other scaffold groups, under ECFP4, SMI-TED and Mordred (PDV on Caco-2, where Mordred is not a base representation; on HLM clearance ECFP4 is not a base representation and its stored features were used).
On hERG K_i any two of the three share on average 0.47 to 0.52 of each molecule's five neighbors, and on the three Biogen datasets and QM9 only 0.13 to 0.21 (Table [REF]).
For 500 random pairs per dataset we found the maximum common substructure (MCS) with RDKit [CIT], allowing 2 seconds per pair and leaving out pairs that ran out of time.
The MCS distance is 1 - n/(a+b-n), where n is the number of atoms in the common substructure and a and b are the numbers of heavy atoms in the two molecules.
Its Spearman correlation with ECFP4 Tanimoto distance ranged from 0.20 (hERG K_i and HLM clearance) to 0.51 (Caco-2 and LogD).
Every method in Section [REF] takes a similarity as input and inherits the dilution described here.
We've identified some issues within the representations and similarities computed over them.
While this calls into question the predictive limits of QSAR and other structure-based modeling, it also calls into question downstream applications of molecular similarity.
Nearest-neighbor methods, where a molecule's neighbors, as measured by similarity, are the inputs to several other processes, are by definition sensitive to the quality of similarity measurements.

They are used within other processes like predicting a molecule's activity using its neighbors' labels, detecting outliers, either ACs or noise, defining an applicability domain by distance to the training set [CIT], grouping molecules into clusters for data splits [CIT], identifying activity cliffs, and, in federated learning, weighting each site's vote on a molecule by that molecule's distance to the site's own data [CIT].
If this measure of similarity, or equivalently distance, is flawed, then all of these downstream applications will feel the effects of it.

Neighbor-based scores compared each label with those of the molecule's k nearest training molecules under Euclidean, Manhattan or cosine distance.
Table [REF] holds only the configurations built on a single representation; those built on an early hybrid are described below.
This study is separate from the sample-removal study of Chapter [REF].
With the neighbor-based scores used as sample weights at strength = 0.1, mean recovery was negative for every representation at both noise levels (Table [REF]).
Of all 860 cleaning configurations, 8 had positive recovery at both noise levels; 6 of these used a single representation, and 4 of those 6 were neighbor-based.
Label smoothing toward neighbor or model estimates gave positive recovery in 5.0\% of configurations at = 0.3 and 0.8\% at = 0.6.
Mean recovery was negative at every weighting and smoothing strength tried, from 0.1 to 0.7.
Judging a label by its neighbors usually made the model worse and rarely helped at both noise levels, but it did not always fail.
The best configuration at = 0.6 was neighbor-based (PDV, Euclidean distance, local variance ratio score) and recovered +17.2\%.
Because noise was added to every training label, the neighbors' labels are noisy too; the exploratory study gave this as the reason label smoothing failed.
Uncertainty-based methods, which use no neighbors, showed potential at lower noise but degraded at higher noise.
Sample weighting did better than label smoothing but usually still hurt, with positive recovery in 14.2\% of configurations at = 0.3 and 4.7\% at = 0.6, and mean recoveries of -22.9\% and -20.9\%.
The study also found neighbors in an early hybrid of 100 PDV and MHG-GNN features, built by greedy forward selection, which is no longer part of the method.
Its mean recovery with neighbor-based scores was -0.9\% at = 0.3 and -3.0\% at = 0.6, with 44.4\% and 27.8\% of configurations positive.
On a single dataset, often very little of a standard representation varies.
On hERG K_i, 1,815 of the 2,048 ECFP4 features take one value in at least 95\% of the 1,412 molecules (Section [REF]).
Several representations also give different molecules, mostly stereoisomers, the same feature vector, and no model can separate those molecules, whatever their labels.
ECFP4 gives 56 of the 1,412 hERG K_i molecules a vector shared with another molecule, all of them stereoisomers (``Molecules with identical feature vectors'').
A distance sums over every feature, so when only a few features matter for the property, the rest dominate the sum (Section [REF]).
Across 70 combinations of dataset and representation, the Spearman correlation between pair distance and label difference was below 0.10 in 44.
Predicting each label from its five nearest neighbors gave a higher Spearman correlation in all 70, so the useful information sits in a few close pairs rather than in the distance as a whole.
In the small sweep of published noise-handling methods, configurations that used a distance did worst under label noise (Section [REF]).
Judging a label by its neighbors' labels usually made the model worse, though one neighbor-based configuration gave the best recovery at the higher noise level (Section [REF]).
The noise was on every training label, so each molecule's neighbors were noisy too.
Chapter [REF] tests neighbor-based detection under other noise conditions.
A representation that avoids these flaws would need five properties (Table [REF]).
Its features would be chosen for the task, using only each fold's training labels.
It would be compact, dropping features that do not vary or do not matter, with the number kept searched rather than fixed.
It would draw on several representations, since each misses information the others capture; plain concatenation does this but is not compact (Chapter [REF], ``Combining representations'').
It would work both as a model input and as a space for similarity.
Finally, it would be traceable: each chosen feature leads back to its representation and can be read chemically wherever the base feature can.
Feature selection cannot fix every flaw.
Molecules identical in every base representation stay identical in the hybrid, and a selected hashed bit still merges every substructure folded into it.
Selection also needs enough labeled molecules to estimate which features matter.
Three limits apply to this chapter.
The sweep of published methods and the neighbor-based cleaning used one dataset, the QM9 HOMO--LUMO gap, and Gaussian noise only.
The sweep also added a distance to methods designed without one, so poor adaptation may explain part of their result.
The cliff counts rest on one similarity threshold, 0.55, and on a gap set so that 15\% of the molecules are cliff molecules.
Chapter [REF] builds the adaptive hybrid representation and asks how to select its features for a given prediction task (Section [REF]).
Every number in this section is a held-out score, in the dataset's own metric, over five outer folds unless stated otherwise.
Most DNN results were computed before the correction of 8 October 2026 (Section [REF]).

On small molecules the hybrid scores better than the best single representation on every dataset, with both downstream models (Table [REF]), and on the six regression datasets it does so on every fold.
On hERG blocking the hybrid is ahead on most folds with each model.
On every small-molecule dataset the hybrid also beats, with both models, the single representation that was best on the held-out molecules, a choice no user could make in advance.
On Caco-2 with the DNN the best single representation in hindsight is PDV, at 0.2980 RMSE, against 0.2775 for the hybrid.
To see what the hybrid draws on, we shuffled each representation's features in turn on the held-out molecules.
On hERG K_i, Caco-2 and MDR1--MDCK efflux, the drop in the hybrid's score is spread about equally over five to seven representations.
No single representation carries as much as a third of it.
On QM9 with LightGBM and on hERG blocking the hybrid leans more on one representation.
It carries most of the score on QM9 and about half on hERG blocking, and the hybrid still beats every single representation.
On antibodies the result differs from one dataset to the next (Table [REF]).
On the anti-VEGF expression scan, with 4,275 variants the largest antibody set, the hybrid is ahead of the best single representation with the SVM on all five folds.
On G the mean gain is the largest in the chapter with both models, though the gain moves by more than its own size from fold to fold.
On EGFR binding, expression titer and AC-SINS self-association the hybrid's mean is higher with both models, while it wins on only two to four of the five folds.
In an antibody representation, as in a molecular fingerprint, the features that matter are few and buried among many that carry nothing.
A language model's embedding of the whole sequence mixes the CDRs that vary with a framework that mostly does not.
Many of the antibody representations in the pools were built for this thesis to separate the two (Table [REF]).
On three antibody datasets the hybrid beats even the single representation that was best in hindsight, and on two of them that representation is one of ours.
On the anti-VEGF expression scan it is the CDR readout of ESM3 with the SVM.
On G it is the mutation features with the SVM and the change from the parent embedding with the DNN.
When each representation's features are shuffled in turn in the G hybrid, the representations built for this thesis carry most of the drop in score with both models, 0.83 of it with the SVM.
On the other antibody datasets they carry at most 0.21, so they matter most where the antibodies differ by defined mutations.
On AC-SINS self-association, the third dataset, the hybrid draws mainly on two antibody language models, IgT5 and AbLang-2.
Across the antibody datasets the hybrids draw on two to four and a half representations by the same measure.
On angiopoietin-2 binding the best representation in hindsight, AntiBERTy, was never ranked first on any fold's training antibodies.
On nanobody thermostability, SMAC colloidal stability, HIC retention and CHO polyreactivity the hybrid adds nothing (Table [REF]).
With the SVM on thermostability and on colloidal stability the two scores are almost equal.
On HIC retention it is behind with the Gaussian process, and here the search picked the same ESM-2 representation on every fold, so the single representation was not the problem.
These datasets also carry label problems of their own.
The thermostability label pools five assays into one, and nearly a third of the CHO polyreactivity labels sit at the assay floor.
On angiopoietin-2 binding the hybrid is higher with both models (Table [REF]), on three of five folds.
Its labels were read off a published heatmap.
Antibody humanness is a task one representation already solves, with a high AUROC for both the single representation and the hybrid, so the hybrid has nothing to add.
On the Buchwald--Hartwig reactions the two models disagree (Table [REF]).
With LightGBM the hybrid lowers the RMSE, and with the random forest it raises it.
Both differences are smaller than how much they vary across folds.
The search drew on only two of the ten representations on every fold: the reaction fingerprint and the change in the MHG-GNN embedding from reactants to product.
The folds hold out whole additives, so on this split the reaction representations carry little that the hybrid could combine.
We have not yet run the experiment that tests whether the best hybrid settings follow measurable properties of a dataset, so here we only describe what each fold's search picked.
Much of what looks like a dataset pattern was fixed in advance by each dataset's search grid (Table [REF]).
The QM9, LogD and hERG blocking searches could use only LightGBM gain.
SMAC colloidal stability, HIC retention, expression titer and CHO polyreactivity searched only budgets wider than their 152 to 198 training antibodies.
Where the grid left a choice, the downstream model moved the pick as much as the dataset did (Figures [REF] and [REF]).
Dataset size did not order the budgets either.
QM9, the largest dataset with 7,982 training molecules per fold, picked 1,000 features on 4 of 5 folds with the DNN, below LogD's 2,000.
Until the cross-dataset experiment runs, which datasets the hybrid helps on is read dataset by dataset from the comparisons above.

With budgets searched up to 8,000 features, the selection bias is small on the larger small-molecule datasets.
On the small antibody datasets the search promises much more than it delivers, by up to 0.1571 Spearman on colloidal stability with the DNN.
On these datasets the folds also often pick a hybrid wider than their own training set, for example on every fold of EGFR binding with the SVM.
With a few thousand molecules the search's internal scores are reliable enough to choose between configurations.
With 150 to 500 training antibodies they are not, so the choice it makes is partly noise.
On permuted class labels, selecting features on the full dataset before cross-validation gave [CIT] an error close to zero, against close to chance with selection redone inside each fold.
Every number in this chapter is scored on samples the search never saw, so the gains above are not this bias.
The bias still exists inside the search, and the numbers above show where it is large: on small datasets, where many configurations are compared on few samples [CIT].
Repeating each fold's search with one more fold of training samples left out makes the held-out score worse on every small-molecule dataset with a result, with both models.
On the regression datasets it is worse by 0.009 to 0.037 RMSE.
The two searches differ in two ways at once: the training samples and the budget each one picks.
So the hybrid gains from more data, but this does not say which of the two changes causes it.

subsection: Selection at a fixed number of features
text: On antibodies random features are beaten at most budgets, but recursive elimination is ahead on G with the SVM and on CHO polyreactivity at every budget.
The number of features the search picks depends on the dataset and on the downstream model.
On Caco-2 the search picked more features for the DNN than for the SVM.
On LogD it picked 2,000 for the DNN on every fold, the top of the grid, so the best width for that model may lie above what was searched.
The SVM's smaller picks fit what Chapter [REF] showed for distances.
A kernel computed over many features is diluted by the ones that carry nothing, while a network can learn to ignore them.
The small antibody sets pick at most a few hundred features on angiopoietin-2 and G.
On expression titer the random forest's pick varies widely between folds, which is the selection noise of the previous section showing up in the budget.
No one budget or representation count would serve every dataset and model, which is why both are searched (Figures [REF] and [REF]).
Across the configurations of a search, the choice of downstream model accounts for more of the variation in score than the budget on most datasets with a result.
On LogD, for example, it accounts for 48.5\% of the variance against 1.4\% for the budget.
The budget still interacts with the model's own settings.
With the SVM on LogD, rat microsomal clearance, MDR1--MDCK efflux and Caco-2, the search picks the same budget on every fold when the SVM's C is 0.01 or 0.1.
On LogD and rat microsomal clearance it picks larger budgets when the SVM is not (C = 10).
A model that is allowed to fit more can use more features.
The width of the DNN does not move its pick in the same way: on LogD it takes the top of the grid at every width.
Scoring candidate hybrids with the downstream model itself, rather than a model of another family, makes almost no difference on small molecules.
On LogD, Caco-2 and hERG K_i with the SVM the three evaluator settings end within a few thousandths of an RMSE unit of each other.
A cheap evaluator ranks candidate feature sets about the same way as the model that will use them, so on these datasets the search does not need the expensive one.
On some antibody datasets it matters.
On EGFR binding the matched evaluator gives 0.3527 Spearman with the SVM against 0.2993 for a LightGBM evaluator.
It is also best with both models on expression titer and colloidal stability.
Using the importance scores again during training does little on small molecules.
The best of the four conditions gains little over the plain hybrid on any small-molecule dataset, and feature scaling makes LogD with the SVM worse.
The selection has already used the importance scores, so on small molecules there is little left for them to add.
On antibodies some condition helps on most datasets, and by more.
Feature scaling takes colloidal stability with the DNN from 0.2607 to 0.3571 Spearman, and keeping the above-median features also helps G with the SVM.
Both act as further regularization on training sets of a few hundred antibodies.
Which condition helps changes from one dataset and model to the next, so none of them is a default.
Choosing fewer features does not replace tuning the model on small molecules.
A hybrid of up to 2,048 features with the SVM's regularization setting tuned beats the search's smaller hybrid at the default setting.
It does so on all four small-molecule datasets with a result, for example 0.4114 against 0.4299 RMSE on LogD.
On nanobody thermostability, G, expression titer and the Buchwald--Hartwig reactions the smaller hybrid is ahead.
The budget and the model's own regularization both control how much the model can fit.
With thousands of molecules the model's setting does that better, and with a few hundred the budget does.
The hybrid can take in a new embedding as one more base representation, and on small molecules it uses it.
Its selected features beat Gaussian random features put in the same places in the hybrid.
They do so for every embedding on Caco-2 and hERG K_i, and for seven or eight of eight on LogD.
On colloidal stability, expression titer and the Buchwald--Hartwig reactions, they do so for fewer than half of the embeddings.
On the two antibody datasets, one more language model of the same sequence adds little.

With 90\% conformal intervals, the hybrid's intervals on small molecules cover close to 90\% of the held-out molecules, as the single representation's do, and are narrower: on LogD with the SVM the mean width falls from 1.652 to 1.403 log units.
On several small antibody datasets the hybrid's intervals cover too few held-out antibodies, fewer than the single representation's, for example on angiopoietin-2 binding and G with the SVM.
The calibration set is part of a training fold of a few hundred antibodies.
The hybrid chosen on those antibodies is optimistic about them, the same selection bias as above.
On one fold of each dataset (Figure [REF]), several hybrids draw on all ten representations in similar amounts, for example on LogD with the DNN and on the anti-VEGF expression scan with the SVM.
Elsewhere one or two representations carry the hybrid.
On EGFR binding almost all of its features come from ESM-2 run on the joined chains.
LogD can be read chemically (Figure [REF]).
The SVM's hybrid picked 372 features on all five folds.
Of these, 38 are Mordred descriptors and 36 are ECFP4 bits.
The rest come from eight representations whose features carry no names.
Among the descriptors are Crippen's calculated logP (SLogP), the number of basic groups (nBase) and several surface areas binned by partial charge (PEOE\_VSA).
There are also counts of secondary amine and aromatic nitrogen environments.
Among the bits are tertiary amine environments, in which a nitrogen is bonded to three carbons (CN(C)C), and aryl chloride environments.
Unlike logP, which counts only the neutral form of a molecule, logD at pH 7.4 counts every charge state.
At that pH a basic amine is largely protonated, which lowers logD below logP.
A model of LogD should therefore need both lipophilicity and basicity.
The hybrid picked both, on every fold, from two different representations.
The features picked are partly the same from fold to fold.
On the stability index of [CIT], the small-molecule hybrids score between 0.27 and 0.50.
The antibody hybrids score between 0.08 and 0.27, and the Buchwald--Hartwig ones fall in the same range.
Many features are correlated within and across representations, so a feature on one fold can stand in for a different one on another.
An index well below 1 therefore does not mean the hybrid is fitting noise.
It does mean a blueprint should be read for what recurs across folds, as for LogD above, rather than from a single fold's list.
On antibodies, features drawn from several language models of one sequence are largely interchangeable, and on a few hundred antibodies which of them is picked changes from fold to fold.
The small-molecule result carries over to the three activity-cliff targets of [CIT], data the hybrid was not developed on.
For all but one of the six target and model pairs, the hybrid has a lower error than the single representation the same search ranked first.
With the DNN on factor Xa it goes from 0.7367 to 0.6612 MAE in log units of activity, lower on all five folds.
The exception is factor Xa with LightGBM, where the hybrid is worse.
These targets have many activity cliffs, which is where a single similarity-based representation struggles most (Chapter [REF]).
On Caco-2, MACCS keys and the WL graph kernel both give some molecules a row that another molecule also has (Table [REF]).
Amino-acid composition does the same to 432 of the 659 variants in the EGFR scan, which differ by single mutations.
None of the hybrids built on these datasets leaves two samples with the same row.
On hERG K_i the graph kernel leaves some molecules sharing a row (Table [REF]).
Adding features from ECFP4 and MHG-GNN takes it from 0.6109 to 0.5715 RMSE with the SVM, lower on all five folds, and no two molecules share a row.
Adding ECFP4 and PDV instead improves it almost as much while some molecules still share a row.
So most of the gain comes from the information the added representations give every molecule, and little from breaking the ties.
Search settings found on LogD were reused on hERG K_i, with the features selected again on hERG K_i.
They beat hERG K_i's best single representation with both models (SVM 0.5888 to 0.5665 RMSE, on all five folds).
They stay behind a search run on hERG K_i itself.
Reusing settings saves the search on the smaller dataset at some cost in error.
Feature selection can run where data cannot be pooled.
When each site holds one family of representations, one feature selection over all families beats both the best single family and the best single representation on Caco-2 and LogD, with both models.
On LogD with the SVM it reaches 0.4382 RMSE, against 0.4598 for the best family, and the best single representation is further behind.
Selecting at each site with an even share of the budget does as well as one selection over all families on every dataset and model.
It can, however, build a different number of features.
So each site can select on its own and send only feature indices.
When each of five sites holds a different representation, one hybrid over all sites beats the best single site on both datasets with both models.
It also beats the collaborator's two ensembles, which combine the sites' predictions, in three of the four dataset and model pairs.
The exception is Caco-2 with the DNN, where the ensembles reach 0.2721 and 0.2730 RMSE against 0.2837 for the hybrid.
With two-class labels and up to 30\% of each site's labels flipped, selecting features at each site beats the collaborator's ensembles and their student model at every flip level on Caco-2.
With the DNN and no flips it reaches an MCC of 0.5085 against 0.3904 for the better ensemble, and it stays ahead with 30\% flipped.
It never beats the same selection made with all molecules pooled, so keeping the data apart still costs something.
With the DNN at 30\% flips the two are almost equal.
Only Caco-2 has finished, with three seeds for the DNN and two for the SVM.
We selected features separately in each of five k-means clusters of Caco-2 and fitted one model on all molecules.
This matches one global selection (0.5289 against 0.5316 MCC with the DNN), while fitting a separate model per cluster is worse.
The clusters agree less on which representations matter than random parts of the same size do, measured by mean rank correlation.
This chapter asked how the best set of features can be selected for a given prediction task (Section [REF]).
The answer is that it depends on the dataset and the downstream model, and that a search can find it.
On every small-molecule dataset the hybrid beats the best single representation with both downstream models, on every fold of the six regression datasets.
It also beats the representation that was best in hindsight.
It does so because the representations carry different information.
On hERG K_i, Caco-2 and MDR1--MDCK efflux the hybrids draw on five to seven of them, and no one of them carries more than 29\% of the drop in score when its features are shuffled.
On small molecules, this supports the hypothesis behind the hybrid, that the feature set is part of the problem.
At the same number of features the hybrid beats recursive elimination and random features on all but one of the small-molecule datasets with a result.
Drawing on several representations beats drawing on the top one alone on most datasets.
How the budget is split matters less than which representations are drawn on.
No single setting suits every dataset and model.
On Caco-2 and LogD the DNN picked more features than the SVM, and the number of representations ranges from two to all ten.
The cheaper internal evaluators are good enough on small molecules but not on some antibody datasets.
The selected features can also be read: on LogD the hybrid picks lipophilicity and basicity on every fold, from two different representations.
On antibodies the hybrid helps for the same reason it helps on small molecules: the features that matter are few and buried in representations of the whole sequence.
On G, AC-SINS self-association and the 4,275-variant expression scan it beats every single representation.
On the first and last of these, the best single representation is one built here to read the regions and mutations that vary.
On the smaller sets its gains are inconsistent, the search's own scores are optimistic, and an ensemble of one model per representation often does better.
The method also runs on reactions, where it gains nothing on the additive split.
It runs on data held at separate sites, where selecting at each site does as well as one selection over all representations.
It also takes in new embeddings added to the pool.
The fourth question asked whether weighting features by their importance improves the hybrid and model training.
In construction, ranking features by importance within each representation is what makes the hybrid work.
In training, using the importance scores again adds little on small molecules and helps on some small antibody datasets, with no condition that works everywhere.
Whether hybrids keep more of their performance under label noise, and whether their features stabilize noise mitigation, are the subjects of Chapters [REF] and [REF].
The hybrid needs data.
Its gains are consistent on datasets of a few thousand samples and inconsistent on datasets of a few hundred.
On those smaller datasets the search's internal scores overstate what the chosen hybrid delivers by up to 0.16 Spearman (Section [REF]), and its prediction intervals cover too few held-out samples.
Most of the antibody datasets in this chapter are of that size.
The antibody results therefore say as much about dataset size as about antibodies, and these datasets cannot separate the two.
Whether the best hybrid settings follow measurable properties of a dataset is the question of the experiment still to be reported in Section [REF].
The hybrid can only select from what the pool offers.
The antibody pools are mostly protein and antibody language models of the same sequence, several of them variants of ESM-2.
The antibody hybrids therefore had few representations of different kinds to combine.
Frozen embeddings also set a ceiling: no signal can be added beyond what the inputs contain.
Integrating many foundation models, each with its own dependencies and hardware, is difficult engineering, and the burden grows with the number of models.
The search is costly and must be rerun when the data, the representations or the downstream model change.
The grid of each dataset was cut to save compute (Section [REF]), so the hybrids reported here are at worst less informative than a full search would find.
The settings found on one dataset carry over to a related one only partly, and we tested this on one pair of datasets.
A downstream model from outside the fixed list of model families gets no matched evaluator.
A full search of one dataset took 0.4 to 38.6 hours of CPU jobs, 8 cores each by default, summed over its 5 outer folds.
A simpler selection is sometimes enough.
Recursive feature elimination over all representations joined beat the hybrid at every budget on G with the SVM and on CHO polyreactivity.
It also beat it on hERG K_i with the DNN at the larger budgets.
On small molecules, tuning the SVM on a wider hybrid did better than a smaller one.
Where one of these is enough, the search costs more than it returns.
Several results are provisional.
Most DNN results were computed before the correction of 8 October 2026.
The Gaussian-process results will change when that model is replaced.
With the DNN, the comparison with PCA at the same number of features disagrees between experiments and waits for the DNN re-runs.
The experiment on adding a new embedding ran on 2,000 molecules of LogD and hERG blocking, and its random control swaps features without a new search.
The separate sites are simulated from one public dataset, so the differences between real sites in curation and chemistry are not tested.
Only Caco-2 has finished the experiment with flipped labels.
This chapter used the hybrid only as input to a model.
Chapter [REF] asks whether a feature set chosen for the task also gives better neighbors, which every method that relies on similarity could use, including the detection of noisy labels.
As in Chapter [REF], distance in a standard representation rises only weakly with the difference in labels.

On the small-molecule datasets, the best of ten representations and distances, picked on the held-out molecules, reaches at most 0.2789 Spearman, on QM9, and varies widely between folds, for example on hERG K_i.
On the small-molecule datasets and Buchwald--Hartwig, no representation has a correlation at or below zero.
On EGFR binding, CHO polyreactivity, AC-SINS self-association and SMAC colloidal stability, at least one representation does.
SMAC colloidal stability is weakest: its best single representation reaches 0.0155 Spearman, and about half of its combinations of representation and distance are at or below zero.
In the distance hybrid, distance tracks label differences more closely on all five small-molecule datasets (Table [REF]).
On LogD the hybrid is higher in every fold, while on Caco-2 it is lower in two folds.
The same holds on all seven antibody datasets and Buchwald--Hartwig, including SMAC colloidal stability.
The predictive hybrids, built for each downstream model rather than for distance, do not always do this.
Some track label differences less closely than their model's best single representation, on Caco-2, EGFR binding, expression titer, SMAC colloidal stability and Buchwald--Hartwig.
On CHO polyreactivity all four predictive hybrids are lower, for example 0.1056 to 0.0644 Spearman for the network's first hybrid.
A hybrid used for distance therefore has to come from the distance search.
Importance weighting on its own closes much of the gap.
On LogD, the single representation with weighting reaches 0.2762 Spearman, which is above the unweighted hybrid (Table [REF]).
On QM9 the weighted single representation stays below the unweighted hybrid.
On both, the weighted hybrid is highest of the three.
The weighted comparison is missing on Caco-2, hERG blocking, hERG K_i, expression titer and SMAC colloidal stability.
The single representation here is the one the nearest-neighbor model ranked first for prediction, not the one whose distance best follows the label.
If we instead pick that representation with hindsight on the held-out molecules, under any of the distances, the distance hybrid is lower on Caco-2.
The similarity hybrid on Caco-2 is higher than that pick.
The same hindsight comparison also goes against the distance hybrid on EGFR binding, expression titer and CHO polyreactivity.
A hybrid's prediction score peaks at more features than the correlation between its distances and label differences does.
On LogD the network's hybrid predicts better at 2,000 features than at 500, while distance in the same hybrid falls from 0.2315 to 0.1535 Spearman.
At the setting fixed before the run, predicting each molecule from its five nearest neighbors is more accurate in the distance hybrid on all five small-molecule datasets (Table [REF]).
The hybrid is better in every fold on LogD, and worse in one fold of five on hERG K_i and Caco-2.
Picking the setting again for each fold does not change this, and the hybrid still wins on all five small-molecule datasets, for example on LogD from 0.6384 to 0.5648 RMSE.
This comparison favors the hybrid (Section [REF]).
On the antibody datasets and Buchwald--Hartwig, the result depends on the comparison.
At the fixed setting the hybrid also wins on most antibody datasets, and loses on G, AC-SINS self-association and Buchwald--Hartwig (Table [REF]).
With the setting picked again for each fold, however, it wins only on EGFR binding, G and SMAC colloidal stability.
It loses on nanobody thermostability, AC-SINS self-association, CHO polyreactivity, expression titer and Buchwald--Hartwig.
The largest gain that holds in both is on SMAC colloidal stability, from 0.0918 to 0.2906 Spearman with the setting picked again.
Multiplying features by their importance mostly helps prediction from nearest neighbors; the exceptions are in bold in Table [REF].
For the other models, weighting gains little or loses.
On hERG K_i the Gaussian process goes from 0.5819 to 0.7115 RMSE, and the support vector regressor also loses there, while on LogD the regressor barely moves.
With neighbor-label features the direction depends on the setting.
On LogD the support vector machine improves with ten neighbors under cosine distance and gets worse with twenty.
Weighting also improves prediction from all representations joined.
With 10 neighbors, weighting by LightGBM gain improves all four regression small-molecule datasets, for example QM9 from 0.5749 to 0.4841 RMSE.
It also helps every antibody dataset and Buchwald--Hartwig with at least one importance method.
It loses with DeepLIFT on Caco-2, and with LightGBM gain on SMAC colloidal stability.
We have not compared the importance weights with shuffled weights, so we cannot say how much of the gain comes from the importance itself.
Whether the hybrid wins depends on the dataset much more than on how the neighbors are found.
Averaged over the other settings, the gain on LogD is similar for each distance and number of neighbors, and the hybrid loses on G under all three distances.
Importance weighting on both sides shrinks the gain on every dataset where the hybrid wins, on LogD from 0.078 to 0.023 RMSE.
Part of what the hybrid does for a distance is therefore what weighting does.
Where the hybrid loses, the spread across folds is larger than the gain, for example on G and AC-SINS self-association.
These datasets have a few hundred training antibodies, against one to eight thousand training molecules for the small-molecule datasets, so we cannot tell size and domain apart here.
The settings the search chose for the hybrid do not line up with winning either.
On LogD and QM9 it picks the same allocation and importance method in every fold, but CHO polyreactivity wins every fold with four different choices.
Retrieval (Section [REF]) shows the same pattern.

On LogD the hybrid's neighbors have closer labels under each distance and number of neighbors, and the hybrid loses on G under all three distances, by less than the spread across folds at the setting fixed before the run.

On the antibody datasets the distance does matter: cosine distance gives the hybrid its smallest lead, and on SMAC colloidal stability it reverses the result, from labels 0.028 closer under Manhattan distance to 0.057 further apart under cosine.
We also tried choosing which molecules to measure next in a hybrid, on hERG K_i and Buchwald--Hartwig only, from three starting sets.
On both the best search is in a hybrid, but on both another hybrid does worse than random picking.
We report activity cliffs on the five small-molecule datasets only.
On the antibody datasets too few held-out antibodies count as cliff antibodies for a score; on G, 11 of the 429 antibodies held out over five folds do.
The rule for held-out molecules is looser than the one that makes 15\% of the training molecules cliff molecules, so their share differs.
It is highest on LogD and hERG blocking, where nearly half of the held-out molecules in some folds are cliff molecules, and lowest on hERG K_i.
On LogD, Caco-2, hERG K_i and hERG blocking, each model's first hybrid beats its best single representation on cliff molecules and on the other molecules alike.
On Caco-2, hERG K_i and hERG blocking the gain is larger on cliff molecules than on the rest; on Caco-2 the network goes from 0.3396 to 0.2881 RMSE on cliff molecules.
On LogD the gain on cliff molecules is slightly smaller than on the rest, but both models gain on them in every fold.
A second run with the small-molecule models flags the same cliff molecules and agrees in direction on all four datasets.
QM9 is harder to read.
The hybrid is better on the other molecules for both models.
On cliff molecules only two folds hold the 10 a score needs, and there the hybrid is worse for both models, for the network from 0.2422 to 0.2798 RMSE.
In each model, the hybrid is better in one of those two folds and worse in the other.
With 48 cliff molecules in all, we draw no conclusion from QM9.
A molecule's distance to its nearest training molecules does rise with the error made on it, but weakly.
The distance hybrid tracks error better for both models on QM9, Caco-2, hERG K_i and LogD.
The largest change is on hERG K_i, from 0.1996 to 0.2761 Spearman with the support vector machine's errors, while on LogD it is small.
On hERG blocking the hybrid tracks error worse for both models.
On nanobody thermostability, G, expression titer, CHO polyreactivity and AC-SINS self-association, the hybrid tracks error better for both models.
It tracks error worse for both on SMAC colloidal stability, where the network goes from 0.1360 to 0.0295 Spearman, and on Buchwald--Hartwig.
On Buchwald--Hartwig, G and expression titer, distance in the single representation does not rise with error at all for either model.
The distance hybrid retrieves neighbors with closer labels on all five small-molecule datasets.
With the setting picked again for each fold, QM9's label gap falls from 0.6008 to 0.3928.
Clustering by k-means agrees with retrieval on hERG blocking, LogD and QM9, where the hybrid's clusters are more coherent at 3, 5 and 10 clusters.
On Caco-2 and hERG K_i the answer changes with the number of clusters, and on Caco-2 the hybrid loses at 3 clusters but wins at 5 and 10.
On the other domains it depends on the dataset.

With the setting picked again, the hybrid retrieves neighbors with closer labels on every antibody dataset except G, where the label gap rises from 1.4386 to 1.5072, and Buchwald--Hartwig is worse too.
Principal components of all representations retrieve better than the hybrid only on EGFR binding, and tie on CHO polyreactivity.
Clustering is mixed.
On EGFR binding and SMAC colloidal stability the hybrid's clusters are less coherent at 3, 5 and 10 clusters, although on SMAC colloidal stability its retrieval still wins.
On nanobody thermostability and CHO polyreactivity the hybrid's clusters are more coherent at every count.
The features a hybrid keeps carry no more label information than principal components of the same number.
On LogD the median, summed over single features, is 1.63 nats for the kept features against 1.68 for principal components, and lower for a random subset.
Chapter [REF] found that distance in standard representations barely rises with the difference in labels.
On the five small-molecule datasets, distance in a hybrid built for distance tracks label differences more closely than in the single representation (Table [REF]).
Prediction from nearest neighbors improves on all five (Table [REF]), at the setting fixed before the run and with the setting picked again.
Neighbors retrieved in the hybrid have closer labels on all five.
On LogD, Caco-2, hERG K_i and hERG blocking, each model's first hybrid also predicts cliff molecules better than its best single representation.
Weighting features by importance does part of the same work without any selection.
On LogD the weighted single representation tracks label differences better than the unweighted hybrid.
Distance in the hybrid tracks prediction error worse on hERG blocking, and the kept features carry no more label information than principal components of the same size.
On the antibody datasets and Buchwald--Hartwig, the result depends on the dataset.
Distance in the hybrid tracks label differences more closely on all of them.

With the setting picked again, prediction from nearest neighbors is worse in the hybrid on nanobody thermostability, AC-SINS self-association, CHO polyreactivity, expression titer and Buchwald--Hartwig.
Retrieval is worse on G and Buchwald--Hartwig.
These losses agree with the central claim of this thesis, that the right input depends on the data, so a hybrid's benefit has to be measured on each dataset.
Four limitations apply.
QM9 has no result for the best number of features, importance weighting in the four models, or choosing which molecules to measure next.
The weighted comparison of distance against label difference is missing on Caco-2, hERG blocking, hERG K_i, expression titer and SMAC colloidal stability.
The comparison with the setting picked again lets the hybrid side choose among more combinations and use importance weighting, so it favors the hybrid.
Held-out molecules are called cliff molecules by a looser rule than training molecules, so the share of cliff molecules differs between the two.
The hybrid and the single representation are scored on the same cliff molecules, so their comparison is not affected.
On QM9 only 48 held-out molecules are cliff molecules, too few to judge.
Methods that find noisy labels by comparing each label with its neighbors' labels rest on the distance studied here.
Chapter [REF] tests whether the hybrid's distance makes noisy labels easier to find and to act on.
Three things hold for every result in this chapter, so we state them once.
Because of time and computational constraints, most results are on the first outer fold only (Section [REF]), and we give the fold count wherever more exist.
Where a method has several settings, such as a share to delete or a strength, we report its best setting on the held-out score.
The single representation and the hybrid it is compared on are picked the same way.
Both picks make every reported gain optimistic.
Third, the network's score changes from one fit to the next.
On QM9 the network's second hybrid scores between 0.3484 and 0.3618 RMSE on the same fold and the same labels, depending on which experiment fitted it.
LightGBM gives one score in every experiment.
A network gain of about 0.01 RMSE or less is inside that spread.
Table [REF] shows how often each group of methods improved the held-out score on the first outer fold.
In it, one condition is one dataset, noise condition, model and method.
A row sorts its conditions by outcome: the method improved both the best single representation and the best hybrid, only one of them, or neither.
Where a method has a control, improving both also means beating it.
Mitigation helps most often under injected damage, and least often on the labels as delivered.
The table counts outer fold 0 only.
Six of its experiments also have results on folds 1 and 2, which it does not count.
It also leaves out MDR1--MDCK efflux, which has 24 conditions on fold 0.
